title: everything happens for a reason
hookLine: the line everyone says after a breakup, and nobody can source

cards: Everything happens for a reason. It gets said after a breakup, a missed flight, a job that fell through. It's on mugs and in captions.
It often gets pinned on Aristotle, but you won't find the line in anything he wrote. So where does it come from, and why does it feel so true, even to people who aren't sure what they believe?

teach.b: Start with the mind. Researchers asked young children why rocks are pointy: because of how they formed, or so animals could scratch on them? Many picked the animals.
Children see purpose everywhere, and adults never fully grow out of it. In one set of studies, adults were asked about big events in their own lives.

Believers often said those events happened for a reason, and so did a surprising number of atheists. A mind that's always reading other people's intentions starts reading them into events, too. Then the old ideas.

Aristotle wrote that nature does nothing in vain: an eye is for seeing. That's about how living things are built, not about your breakup. The Stoics went further and saw the whole universe ordered by reason.

Many religions speak of providence, God at work in what happens, often in ways no one can see at the time. Those are beliefs, held by serious people for a very long time, and no experiment can settle them.
And here's the part that works either way. Why did this happen? often has no answer you can reach.
What now? always does. Whether or not there's a reason built in, there's a meaning you can make with what comes next.

how: People make sense of hard events in many ways: through faith in providence, through Stoic or Buddhist reflection, or simply by asking what to do next. Counselors often help people find meaning after a loss without asking them to believe the loss was planned.

games.q: where the feeling comes from — tap the pairs.
p: God at work in what happens
the question that always has an answer

s: Aristotle said everything happens for a reason
the line isn't in his writing. he said nature does nothing in vain: an eye is for seeing.
in one set of studies, many atheists also said life events happened for a reason
believers said it more often, but the feeling isn't only religious.
an experiment has settled whether there's a plan behind events
that's a belief no experiment can settle. what's been studied is why we feel it.

games.q: young kids are asked why rocks are pointy: because of how they formed, or so animals can scratch on them. what do many of them pick?
o: so animals can scratch on them.
games.why: the animals. minds reach for purpose first. adults do it too, just about bigger things.

games.q: put the farmer's year in order.

practice: One breath with the bell. Bring to mind one thing from this year you still can't explain. Don't try to.
Breathe in with it. As you breathe out, let the question turn from why to what now. No answer needed yet.

wordCard.voice: Meant to be. A feeling nearly every mind makes, and, for many people, a belief. First word on your strand.

orig.note: Greek, telos: an end, a purpose. Aristotle's word for what a thing is for; English teleology comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: not why, but what now. It works whatever you believe about the why. See you tomorrow.
